title: Points on a circle
objectives: Find the chance that random points on a circle lie in one semicircle.

screens.title: Two points
screens.prose: Two points fall uniformly on a circle. A sits at 0°; slide B round. The shaded half starts at one point and runs anticlockwise for 180°.

derive.caption: B is {{b}}° round from A: {{b <= 180 ? "the half starting at A holds both" : "the half starting at B holds both"}}.

screens.question: What is the chance two random points lie in one semicircle?

options.why: You fixed the half that starts at A. When B misses it, the half that starts at B holds A.
That is the answer for three points. Two points always fit.

hints.text: Slide B all the way round.
Either A's half or B's half holds both.
So the chance is 1.

feedback.correct: Two points always fit in some semicircle.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide B past 180° and watch which half is shaded.

byKey.half: You counted only the half that starts at A. A semicircle may start at either point.

explain.text: Whatever the angle between them, one of the two halves starting at A or at B holds both. So the chance is 1. With three points it is not.

screens.title: A third point
screens.prose: Now three points. Fix the half that starts at A and runs anticlockwise. B and C are independent, uniform on the circle.

derive.caption: {{b <= 180 && c <= 180 ? "B and C are both in the half starting at A" : "The half starting at A misses B or C"}}.

screens.question: What is the chance B and C both land in the half that starts at A? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Each of B and C lands in a given half with chance $\tfrac12$.
They are independent.
$\tfrac12 \times \tfrac12$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the chances for B and for C.

byKey.one: That is one point. Both B and C must land in the half.
byKey.cube: You included A. A starts the half, so it is inside for certain.

explain.text: A starts the half, so only B and C are random. Each lands in it with chance $\tfrac12$, so both do with chance $\tfrac14$.

screens.title: Any point can start
screens.prose: Slide all three points. When they fit in one semicircle, it is shaded. One point starts it: the point just after the largest gap.

let.mid: a + b + c - min(a, b, c) - max(a, b, c)

derive.caption: Largest gap {{round(gm)}}°: {{gm >= 180 ? "one semicircle holds all three" : "no semicircle holds all three"}}.

screens.question: What is the chance three random points lie in one semicircle? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: A starts a good half with chance $\tfrac14$. So do B and C.
Only one point can start the half that holds the others.
The three cases are disjoint: $3 \times \tfrac14$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the chance for each point to be the one that starts the half.

byKey.fixed: That is only A starting the half. B or C can start it too.
byKey.coin: A guess of a half. Count the three disjoint starts.

explain.text: Each point starts a half holding the others with chance $\tfrac14$. At most one point can, so the three events are disjoint. They add to $\tfrac34$.

screens.title: Four points
screens.prose: The same argument with four points. Here A starts a half that holds B, C and D.

state.caption: A starts the shaded half, and the other three fall in it.

screens.question: What is the chance four random points lie in one semicircle? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Fix the starting point: the other three must fall in its half.
That has chance $(\tfrac12)^3 = \tfrac18$.
Four disjoint starts: $4 \times \tfrac18$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the chance for one start by the number of points.

byKey.one-start: That is A starting the half. Any of the four can.
byKey.three: That is the three-point answer. A fourth point makes it harder to fit.

explain.text: The three others fall in the half starting at a given point with chance $\tfrac18$. Four disjoint starts give $\tfrac12$.

screens.title: The centre inside
screens.prose: Join the three points into a triangle. The centre $O$ is inside exactly when no semicircle holds all three.

let.mid: a + b + c - min(a, b, c) - max(a, b, c)

derive.caption: {{gm >= 180 ? "One semicircle holds all three: O is outside" : "No semicircle holds them: O is inside"}}.

screens.question: What is the chance the triangle holds the centre? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: The centre is outside when all three fit in one half.
That has chance $\tfrac34$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the semicircle chance from 1.

byKey.same: That is the chance the centre is outside. Take it from 1.

explain.text: If one half holds all three, the triangle sits on one side of a diameter and misses the centre. Otherwise it holds it. So the chance is $1 - \tfrac34 = \tfrac14$.

screens.title: The coin-flip answer
screens.prose: Three random points on a circle. A candidate says at once: "each point is in any half with chance a half, so a half."
screens.question: What is the chance the three lie in one semicircle?

options.why: You gave a coin-flip answer. Fix the start point: each of the three starts a good half with chance $\tfrac14$.
You let only A start the half. B or C can start it too, and the three cases are disjoint.
You argued from two points. The third can land in the gap opposite the other two.

hints.text: Which point starts the half, going anticlockwise?
Each of the three does with chance $\tfrac14$.
Disjoint cases add: $\tfrac34$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Condition on which point starts the semicircle.

byKey.half: You answered with a coin flip. The half is not fixed in advance, so more layouts fit.

explain.text: The half is not fixed: any point may start it. Fixing the start and adding over the three starts gives $\tfrac34$. The blurted $\tfrac12$ fixes nothing and checks nothing.

screens.title: The method
screens.prose:
Fix the point that starts the semicircle, going anticlockwise. The other $n - 1$ points each land in its half with chance $\tfrac12$. Only one point can start it, so the $n$ cases add:

$$P(n \text{ points in a semicircle}) = \frac{n}{2^{n-1}}.$$
screens.question: Why may we add the $n$ cases?

options.text: At most one point starts a half that holds all the others

options.why: Independent events multiply. We add because the cases cannot happen together.
Each case has chance $(\tfrac12)^{n-1}$, and equal chances alone do not let us add.

hints.text: Adding needs events that cannot happen together.
Could A and B both start a half holding everyone?
Then each would sit within 180° anticlockwise of the other, which is impossible.

feedback.correct: The cases are disjoint, so their chances add.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether two points could both start such a half.

explain.text: If A starts such a half, every other point lies within 180° anticlockwise of A. Then B cannot have A within 180° anticlockwise of itself. So the cases are disjoint and add.

screens.title: Any number of points
screens.prose: With $n$ points, fix the start and use the $n$ disjoint starts.
screens.question: Write the chance that $n$ random points lie in one semicircle.

hints.text: One start: the other $n - 1$ points each have chance $\tfrac12$.
That is $(\tfrac12)^{n-1}$.
Times $n$ starts: $\dfrac{n}{2^{n-1}}$.

feedback.correct: $\dfrac{n}{2^{n-1}}$: 1 for two points, $\tfrac34$ for three, $\tfrac12$ for four.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the chance for one start by $n$.

byKey.one-start: That is one fixed start. Any of the $n$ points can start the half.
byKey.power-n: You raised $\tfrac12$ to the $n$. The start point is inside for certain, so only $n - 1$ points are random.

explain.text: One start leaves $n - 1$ random points, each in the half with chance $\tfrac12$. The $n$ starts are disjoint. So the chance is $n/2^{n-1}$.

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Three puzzles at about 3 minutes each, 9 in all; keep your own time. Points fall uniformly on a circle. Four decimal places.
screens.question: Fill in the three answers.

rows: Five points: chance they lie in one semicircle
Four points: chance their quadrilateral holds the centre
Three points: chance their triangle is obtuse

hints.text: A polygon on the points holds the centre when they are not in one semicircle.
A triangle is obtuse exactly when its points lie in a semicircle: $\tfrac34$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r2c1: Check the obtuse triangle: the obtuse angle faces an arc of more than 180°.

explain.text: Five points give $5/16$, and the quadrilateral holds the centre with chance $1 - \tfrac12 = \tfrac12$. An angle is obtuse when the arc opposite it exceeds 180°. Then all three fit in the shorter arc, so the chance is $\tfrac34$.

screens.title: Follow-up: a sphere
screens.prose: You found the triangle holds the centre with chance $\tfrac14$. The interviewer asks: four random points on a sphere. What is the chance their tetrahedron holds the centre?
screens.question: What is the chance? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Draw a line through the centre and each point. Each point could have been at either end of its line.
That gives $2^4 = 16$ equally likely layouts.
Exactly two of the 16 hold the centre, a layout and its mirror image: $\tfrac{2}{16}$.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac{2}{16} = \tfrac18$, so the four lie in one hemisphere with chance $\tfrac78$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Flip each point to the other end of its line through the centre.

byKey.circle: That is the circle's answer. One more dimension adds one more point and halves it again.
byKey.hemi: That is the chance all four fit in a hemisphere, the opposite event.

explain.text: Flipping points through the centre gives 16 equally likely layouts, and exactly two hold the centre. So the chance is $\tfrac18$. On the circle the same count gives $\tfrac28 = \tfrac14$, as you found.

screens.title: Trades round the clock
screens.prose: A toy model. A currency desk trades 24 hours a day, and the clock face is a circle. Three trades land at independent uniform times.
screens.question: What is the chance some 12-hour window, perhaps across midnight, holds all three? Give four decimal places.

widget.label: Chance
widget.accept: 3/4: a 12-hour window is a semicircle of the clock

hints.text: A 12-hour window is half the clock.
So this is three points in a semicircle.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac34$: three points in a semicircle of the clock.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Treat the day as a circle and use $n/2^{n-1}$.

byKey.fixed: You used the fixed halves, midnight to noon and noon to midnight. A window may start at any time.

explain.text: The clock wraps, so a 12-hour window is a semicircle. Three trades fit in one with chance $\tfrac34$. The fixed halves give only $2 \times \tfrac18 = \tfrac14$, a different question.

ideas: Fix the point that starts the semicircle; the others each land in its half with chance $\tfrac12$.
Only one point can start it, so the $n$ cases are disjoint and add.
The triangle holds the centre, and is acute, exactly when the points are not in one semicircle: $\tfrac14$.
summary.trap: Answering $\tfrac12$ for three points. The half is not fixed: any of the three can start it.

quiz.prose: Six points fall uniformly on a circle.
quiz.question: What is the chance they lie in one semicircle? Give four decimal places.

byKey.power-n: You used $6/2^6$. Only five points are random once the start is fixed.
byKey.one-start: That is one fixed start, $(\tfrac12)^5$. Multiply by the six starts.

explain.text: Six disjoint starts, each with chance $(\tfrac12)^5$: $\tfrac{6}{32} = \tfrac3{16}$.

quiz.prose: Three points fall uniformly on a circle.
quiz.question: What is the chance all three lie in the top half, above the horizontal diameter? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. This half is fixed in advance, so each point must land in it.

byKey.some: That is for some semicircle. Here the half is fixed.
byKey.two: You fixed one point as the start. Here no point starts the half; all three are random.

explain.text: A fixed half gives each point chance $\tfrac12$, independently: $\tfrac18$. Letting the half move is what raised it to $\tfrac34$.

quiz.prose: Three points fall uniformly on a circle and form a triangle.
quiz.question: What is the chance the triangle is acute?

options.why: That is the chance it is obtuse: the points lie in a semicircle.
A guess of a half. An acute triangle holds the centre.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac14$: acute exactly when it holds the centre.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. An acute triangle on a circle holds the centre.

explain.text: A triangle is acute when no semicircle holds its vertices, which is when it holds the centre. That chance is $1 - \tfrac34 = \tfrac14$.
